Recent findings suggest that raya Foundations is a upcoming platform team that owns the shared foundation every other eng team builds on - AI infra (LLM gateway, model routing, spend tracking, code review agents), server architecture, shared libs and dev tooling, CI, security remediation. We own our own roadmap, but our goal is to listen to other developers' needs and take on work that makes our apps safer and easier to build in.

As a Senior Server Engineer on Foundations you'll drive server architecture modernization and build the AI tooling the whole eng team uses. Small team, huge surface area. ~80% roadmap, ~20% keeping the lights on. Node.js + TypeScript at consumer scale.

The ideal candidate has 5+ years of experience, has been the technical leader on past teams, thinks like an owner, builds with AI (not just alongside it), and would rather fix it for everyone than just for themselves.

We offer comprehensive medical and dental coverage, $50 a day food delivery budget, equity based employment, a great culture, learning opportunities, unlimited vacation, 12 weeks paid parental leave, and we pay all employees $1,000 a year to go somewhere in the world that they've never been because of our values of human connection, empathy, and curiosity.

Platform Ownership: Collaborate, build, and lead key components of the shared foundation every Raya engineering team builds on: AI infrastructure (LLM gateway, model routing, spend tracking, code review agents), server architecture, shared libraries, developer tooling, and CI.

According to recent reports, architecture: Drive server architecture modernization. Write the tech specs, make the trade-offs ourselves, plan the work so it ships safely, and see it through to adoption across engineering!

AI Tooling: Build and roll out the AI-collaborative development tooling Raya engineers use every day, from model routing and eval harnesses to cloud agents that review code and catch slop, and set the standards for how we use it.

Engineering Standards: Set the bar the rest of engineering follows through design reviews, code review, and the docs that let other teams build with confidence.

It has been revealed that operational Excellence: Own the full Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) for what you build: CI/CD, observability and alarm coverage, security remediation, and a healthy, blameless on-call rotation. Be an escalation point for deep production debugging.

Mentorship: Help engineers grow through pairing, code review, and direct feedback.

5+ years of hands-on experience building and operating production server software, with a track record of delivering scalable and maintainable systems and growing into a technical leader within your organization.

Demonstrated expertise in system design, architecture, and mastery in Node.js and TypeScript.

Proven experience in building and scaling backend systems in production at a startup or fast-moving environment.

Hands-on with MongoDB and/or PostgreSQL in production, including performance tuning.

Experience owning platform, infrastructure, or developer-productivity work that other teams depend on (shared libraries, CI/CD, dev tooling, observability, or security remediation) and driving its adoption.

Has built and shipped products with LLMs or AI agents in production, beyond a chat wrapper.

Enthusiasm around upcoming AI tools and frameworks - and a willingness to quickly adopt emerging best practices.

Modernizer: You've led a large architecture migration across a codebase other teams depend on, and you got it adopted.

AI Infrastructure: Experience with LiteLLM, Amazon Bedrock, or similar model-routing layers, and with prompt engineering, evals, or fine-tuning in production.

Infrastructure-fluent: Comfortable with AWS, Docker/Kubernetes, and CI/CD, and with the security & infra side of running a consumer product at scale.

Leverage-minded: You'd rather fix it for everyone than just for yourself. You build the tools, workflows, and habits that maximize team velocity, and you measure whether they worked.

Empathetic Leader: You naturally resonate with colleagues, consumers, and collaborative teams, fostering a culture of understanding and innovation.

Bias toward shipping and iteration: You're able to build swiftly, learn, and refine in short cycles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we love fisherman sweaters for the same reason we love a great martini: They’re classic, and they’re comforting.
  • Now, it’s crucial to remember that when it comes to the backstory of most garments, there tends to be a lot of lore mixed in with the genuine history.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we love fisherman sweaters for the same reason we love a great martini: They’re classic, and they’re comforting. A proper fisherman knit brings the whole winter wardrobe into alignment. The chunky texture instantly upgrades jeans and boots, warmth doesn’t sacrifice style, and that easy, rugged-prep vibe that works at the office as well as it does on the couch. In other words, it’s the rare cold-weather staple that’s as practical as it is handsome.

Now, it’s crucial to remember that when it comes to the backstory of most garments, there tends to be a lot of lore mixed in with the genuine history. That mentioned, here’s how the story generally goes. Traditional fisherman sweaters hail from Ireland, where in the late 1800s to the mid-1900s, they were popular for men who had to work long hours on fishing boats. Usually, fisherman sweaters were hand-knit by their wives or by local artisans, and they were always designed to be sturdy and warm, keeping the wind and chill out. Cable-knit patterns became popular for fisherman sweaters. You might know these sweaters as Aran sweaters, referencing the Aran Islands, where the textured design has become a specialty.

In 2026, you probably don’t need a fisherman sweater to keep you warm while you’re on the water off Ireland’s west coast. (Or maybe you do! We don’t know your story.) However, you do need a fisherman sweater for the sheer coziness and looks they provide, though. Our favorite options of all time are below, tested and reviewed by Esquire editors (with some photographed on Esquire’s editor in chief, Michael Sebastian). Anyway, these fisherman sweaters are seriously making us want to take some fishing lessons. Anyone know where we can do that?

According to recent reports, you don’t need to break the bank for a high-quality fisherman sweater that’ll last you years to come. Quince is proof. Crafted from organic cotton, this thick, warm sweater is a perfect layering piece for winter—put a tee or a button-down underneath, a topcoat or a puffer on top, and you’re golden. The rib detailing offers some extra texture and style, and relaxed raglan sleeves offer more freedom of movement.

Ok, so the pictured sweater is no longer in stock. The cable knit rollneck was seasonal, but there is always a fisherman-y option in the collection. Honestly, whichever J. Crew rollneck hits this bar at any point in time, that’s likely my favorite fisherman sweater of the moment.

Sources indicate that L.L. Bean crafts a classic fisherman sweater to a tee. It has everything you’d want in the style: a thick, heavyweight fabric that carries some structure with it; a cable-knit design; and thick cotton yarn that keeps the chill out and the warmth in. This style is a go-to for something timeless without too much fuss or frill. It has a slim fit, so if you want something baggier, more classically cut, make sure to size up.

It has been revealed that okay, hear me out—this isn’t your traditional fisherman sweater, but you can make a damn good excuse for Polo Ralph Lauren’s ultra-soft, ultra-luxe cable-knit sweater when you feel how unbelievably plush this is. This is the fisherman sweater you go to when you want something distinctly elevated and chic but you still want to have a cable-knit design and a fit you can dress down with joggers and slides.

You may already know that we at Esquire have an affinity for shawl collar cardigans. With their laid-back Western vibes and classic Americana silhouette, shawl collar cardigans look handsome on just about any guy. One of our favorites is this fisherman style from Filson. It’s made from thick, warm cotton and features a classic button front and ribbing on the hem and cuffs.

If you, like commerce editor Luke Guillory, aren’t into the super chunky fisherman sweaters and are looking for something a little more lightweight that you can easily layer, this Buck Mason pick should be right up your alley. Luke has even endorsed the style, lauding the sweater for its warm yet lightweight feel, perfect not-too-boxy but not-too-slim cut, and durable cotton that can be machine washed and still not miss a beat.

Sources indicate that this gorgeous wool fisherman sweater is from Finisterre, a surf clothing brand from Cornwall, England, so it’s specifically made for cold, windy days on the water. It’s made from 100 percent heavyweight, pure new wool with a natural crimp, which means it creates natural pockets of air to help insulate you (even if you’re not on the water). One writer indicates it’s one of his go-to winter sweaters.

Brooks Brothers’ woolly sweater is so damn good I might just have to take up the art of fishing to pay proper tribute to it. With a soft and cozy yet breathable wool fabric and cable-knit pattern, this relaxed style puts a contemporary spin on the traditional fisherman sweater. It’s warm, soft, and stylish, and it looks just as good with dress pants and loafers as it does with jeans and sneakers.

Begg x Co’s Isla cashmere sweater is another fantastic, high-quality cashmere option. It’s just oppressively beautiful. Begg x Co operates its own mills in Scotland, which shows up in the world-class materials and construction, but the vibe isn’t overly capital-F-Fashion the way some French or Italian luxury brands can feel. It’s timeless, understated luxury. Made from 8‑ply cashmere, it lands in a perfect mid-weight sweet spot for fall and winter: substantial and warm without being bulky. It’s definitely quite pricey, but you’re paying for the highest level of quality and finish.

Recent findings suggest that this sweater from Ghiaia Cashmere is divine, surprising considering the brand is based out of southern California. The mock neck is the star here—cozy without the bulk of a turtleneck—and the rich brown color is lovely (though it also comes in a clean cream if you want something lighter). A chest pocket adds a surprisingly practical touch, making it feel more functional than you’d ever expect a sweater to be.

In a recent development, it took me until I turned 30 to realize I was a vest guy. Turns out a fleece vest was the key to non-bulky winter layering. It’s what I was needing this whole time, a cornerstone piece. It gets me through the crisp fall mornings and it’s easy to shed for my afternoon walk in the sunshine. Now, I can’t get through a winter without adding another to my collection.

Versatility is the name of the game here. You can dress up any fleece vest with a button-up and breathable chinos, or keep it casual with, say, a long-sleeved tee and some jeans. And really, it’s the only thing that can fit between a bulky sweater and a winter jacket.

Industry observers note that there are tons of fleece vests on the market, so which one do you choose? Well, you don’t have to choose just one for starters. I like to have a couple around in different colors and weights, depending on the weather and my outfit choice. So regardless of if you’re on your first one, or it’s time for your fiftieth, you can shop these nine handpicked fleece vests that I and our other editors swear by.

Basics don’t get more durable than Patagonia. This is your timeless, basic option that'll last you many winters to come. Secure it in one of six versatile colors.

In addition to an adjustable waist, three pockets, and a full front zip, this vest is made from recycled fabrics, so you can have peace of mind knowing that you're doing good while looking good.

Wear it open, wear it zipped. Wear it over a long-sleeved tee or a sweater or a button-down; this is the affordable vest that’s ready for anything.

Industry observers note that if you don’t know where to start, I’m going all in on Columbia. With a collared neck and thick, cozy fleece, this top layer is made for chilly days and windy nights.

Why pay over $500 for a fleece vest from Canada Goose? Why indeed. Probably because you want the softest Italian-spun Poly Cotton Fleece and are actually able to feel the difference. It’s got everything you’d want, including a chest pocket.

Recent findings suggest that made from recycled scraps of Smartwool’s Merino wool, this is the softest fleece vest that won’t cost you $500. The rest of the materials are recycled and reprocessed too, so you get a dash of peace of mind with your comfort.

It has been revealed that when you look at vests like this, you think North Face. The Glacier Fleece is an especially light option, perfect for the days when you need more than three layers.

Recent findings suggest that listen, even I admit that the fleece vest isn’t always the most fashionable choice. And frankly some of them look better zipped up than others. The Pelican and Treeline Green variants of this Patagonia vest are at the top of that list.

Industry observers note that at this point, what more can I do aside from giving one more cozy, cheap option. This one from Quince cleans up nice.

Clutch helps credit unions launch digital lending and account opening. As a Senior Implementation Engineer, you're the product specialist who solves the hardest technical problems on those projects.

Industry observers note that you specialize in one Clutch product and cross-train on a second. You join each project at key moments and whenever it needs something beyond the default setup. An Engagement Manager owns each project and the relationship with the credit union.

This role fits someone who can diagnose a complicated setup, explain it to a non-technical audience and decide when a request is worth building.

Diagnose complicated setups and find working answers through configuration, mapping, integration design and workarounds.

Design and build non-standard configuration, core mapping and integrations.

According to recent reports, decide whether a requested change is worth making. When it isn't, say no, explain why and offer an alternative.

Own the testing strategy and lead live testing sessions with credit union teams.

Advise our implementation team on what's possible, what needs a workaround and what's a true product gap. File clear tickets with our product and engineering teams for the gaps.

Help write and improve our best-practice default setup, workbooks and test scripts with our Product and Engineering teams.

Coach Engagement Managers to run standard setup themselves.

Use AI to speed up your work, and standardize what works with the team.

According to recent reports, work on many projects at once. Occasional onsite visits with customers.

In a recent development, our Professional Services team implements Clutch for our credit union customers. Every project starts from a best-practice default, and we change it when the change improves the credit union's outcome. We test the setup with the credit union and take them live. Our top metric is customer success through renewal and expansion. We look for people with high agency, sound judgment and a strong technical foundation, who keep teammates informed.

Industry observers note that our tech giant is growing promptly, and so is our team. We're looking for people who want to help shape a world-class delivery motion.

Learn our default setups, decision log and the core and vendor systems around your product.

Join your first projects alongside a tenured Implementation Engineer.

Complete onboarding and lead the technical design on several projects.

Handle your first non-standard configurations and integrations on your own.

Be the go-to person for your product area.

Contribute to our default setups, workbooks and test scripts.

Coach Engagement Managers on standard setup.

5+ years of experience in implementation, solutions engineering or technical consulting, ideally in fintech or banking software.

According to recent reports, 2+ years integrating with web APIs. You read and write code (Python, JSON, JavaScript or similar), work comfortably in GitHub and the terminal, and debug payloads yourself.

A record of diagnosing complex setups and finding working answers without engineering work.

Sound judgment on which changes are worth making, and the confidence to say no and explain why.

A grasp of why a product works the way it does and what it does for a customer's business.

A named result from using AI in your work, such as time saved or a faster diagnosis.

According to recent reports, comfort with ambiguity. You build a plan, tracker or checklist when none exists.

The ability to explain technical concepts clearly to non-technical audiences.

According to recent reports, you communicate proactively. You flag risks early and keep Engagement Managers and customers informed.

The ability to keep many projects moving in the same week.

Experience with core banking or credit union core systems, Alloy, Stripe, Plaid or ACH.

Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance intends.

As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

  • Micorosft has unveiled that it's redesigning Copilot, the company's all-encompassing AI assistant, so consumers can hand off complex tasks, build tools by describing what they need, and assign work to an agent that keeps going after they log off.
  • The new Copilot experience has three main parts: Home, Code, and Autopilot.
  • Recent findings suggest that home puts Chat and Copilot Cowork together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Micorosft has unveiled that it's redesigning Copilot, the company's all-encompassing AI assistant, so consumers can hand off complex tasks, build tools by describing what they need, and assign work to an agent that keeps going after they log off.

The new Copilot experience has three main parts: Home, Code, and Autopilot. It also brings Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into the Copilot app. For people, the pitch is simple: Start a task in one place and stay there as it grows from a quick question into a document, an app, or a longer-running project. Most of the new capabilities are still rolling out or in preview.

Recent findings suggest that home puts Chat and Copilot Cowork together. Chat remains the place for quick answers, research, and drafts. Cowork handles work a user wants to delegate, such as preparing a briefing or pulling together a response to a request for proposals. Microsoft said Copilot eventually will route requests to Chat, Cowork, or Code on its own.

According to recent reports, office in Copilot will allow owners to create a Word document, Excel workbook, or PowerPoint deck without leaving that experience. The files remain editable in the regular Office apps, and colleagues can work on them at the same time. Someone building a presentation, for example, could draw on a workbook, draft the slides, and keep refining both files from within Copilot.

Code is aimed at people who need a tool but might never open a development environment. A user can describe a tracker, dashboard, app, or workflow in plain language and have Copilot build it. Microsoft calls these "small, purpose-built solutions." The feature uses the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot and runs in a sandboxed environment. A separate Copilot Managed Runtime, now in preview, lets organizations host and share the resulting apps within Microsoft 365.

Then there is Autopilot, previously known as Scout. It is designed for work that does not end with a single response: following a discussion, checking in with stakeholders, or keeping a project moving over several days. "Give it a name, a role, and a goal," Microsoft noted. Autopilot runs in the cloud and has its own identity, memory, and workspace in the customer's tenant. Microsoft said its actions are subject to permissions, auditing, and organizational controls.

Those longer-running tasks also change how customers pay for Copilot. In a separate pricing post, Microsoft stated everyday work in Chat and Microsoft 365 apps will remain covered by a per-user subscription. Cowork, Code, and Autopilot will be billed separately through usage-based Copilot Credits. A Copilot user subscription will still be needed to access those features.

For enterprise customers, the features that charge by usage will stay off until an admin sets up a spending policy in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Microsoft mentioned there will be no charges before then. Admins can set budgets for the whole organization or for specific groups, limit how much individual owners can spend, and get alerts when costs approach a set amount. Reports will show who is using the features and which tasks are driving costs.

Industry observers note that microsoft is bringing Code and Copilot Managed Runtime under those cost controls alongside Cowork. Copilot Studio agents are expected to follow in October. Before turning the features on for more employees, IT departments will need to decide who can use them, how much they can spend and which tasks are worth the extra cost.

In a recent development, home and Code will begin rolling out through Microsoft's Frontier early access program in the coming weeks. Code's Frontier rollout starts at the end of September, when Autopilot also expands to private preview.

For more information, visit the Microsoft site.

AI Leaders Warn of Risks at United Nations Security Council Briefing

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face recently joined AI researcher Yoshua Bengio at the United Nations headquarters in Upcoming York on September 23 to warn the UN Security Council about the security risks of increasingly capable AI.
  • They did not offer a single initiative for managing those risks.
  • France, which held the Security Council's rotating presidency, convened the meeting on AI and international security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face recently joined AI researcher Yoshua Bengio at the United Nations headquarters in Upcoming York on September 23 to warn the UN Security Council about the security risks of increasingly capable AI.

They did not offer a single initiative for managing those risks. Bengio called for licensing and independent safety reviews. OpenAI's Sam Altman proposed common standards that countries could adopt through their own laws. Anthropic's Dario Amodei urged AI developers to slow down when safety work cannot keep pace. Hugging Face's Clément Delangue warned that limiting access to capable systems could leave defenders at a disadvantage.

France, which held the Security Council's rotating presidency, convened the meeting on AI and international security. The discussion exposed a difficult question for governments: how to oversee technology that crosses borders when countries disagree about who should set the rules.

Sources indicate that bengio, co-chair of the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, challenged the idea that competition forces companies to keep building more powerful systems. "The race is not a law of nature: it is the product of choices," he noted in his published remarks. "They've told us they would slow down if they could. They can.".

It has been revealed that he called on developers to show independent experts that frontier systems are safe to train and deploy. He also proposed incident reporting, licensing, and liability insurance. Bengio identified catastrophic misuse, concentrated power, and the loss of human control as risks that require international cooperation.

Altman acknowledged the danger of moving too quickly. "We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future," he noted, according to remarks published by OpenAI. Decisions about AI's direction "cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," he added.

According to recent reports, altman proposed complementary national and international standards to measure frontier AI capabilities, assess risks, and test safeguards. He stated countries should be able to compare evidence and verify commitments. He also called for faster reporting of serious incidents and secure channels for sharing emerging threats. Such standards should accommodate both open and closed models without favoring established companies, he said.

Amodei made a more direct commitment about the pace of Anthropic's releases: "We will slow down as much as necessary," he told the council. He identified two principal concerns: the misuse of AI to develop biological weapons and the possibility that advanced systems could outstrip developers' ability to control them.

Industry observers note that the Anthropic chief proposed placing outside evaluators inside AI companies with access comparable to employees. He suggested that governments begin with a narrow agreement against using AI to make biological weapons, then develop ways to evaluate models and verify commitments across borders. He also called for common testing standards and a system for notifying other countries of significant AI incidents.

Sources indicate that delangue drew on a July incident in which Hugging Face disclosed an AI agent cyberattack. He called for stronger monitoring and disclosure, but argued that safety also depends on giving defenders access to capable tools. The central danger, he said, was "asymmetry of powerful AI" between attackers and defenders, large companies and everyone else, and wealthy countries and the rest of the world. His team used an open-source model while responding to the attack, he said.

Sources indicate that the U.S. government opposed a broader international regulatory role. White House science adviser Michael Kratsios told the council that countries should develop their own ability to use and govern the technology. In the U.S. statement, he rejected newly introduced global governance structures and used the phrase "superintelligence, formerly known as AI," adopting President Donald Trump's terminology from his General Assembly speech the previous day.

The four AI briefers differed on how far oversight should go and how widely capable systems should be available. They agreed on a narrower point: Governments need better ways to understand what advanced AI systems can do and to detect when safeguards fail.

Use AI to speed up your work, and standardize what works with the team.

Work on many projects at once. Occasional onsite visits with customers.

Join your first projects alongside a tenured Implementation Engineer.

Handle your first non-standard configurations and integrations on your own.

Sound judgment on which changes are worth making, and the confidence to say no and explain why.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Class CrunchLabs, the suite of free curriculum resources from NASA engineer turned YouTube science communicator Mark Rober, has released its first two courses on YouTube.

Designed in partnership with the National Science Teaching Association, the standards-aligned "Carnival of Collisions: Contact Forces" and "Mission MagLev: Electric & Magentic Forces" courses offer free video lessons, guided activities, and supplemental teaching resources for grades 6-8.

Class CrunchLabs was rolled out last year to offer free hands-on science curriculum resources including teaching guides, classroom slides, student readings and handouts, assessments, and instructional videos featuring Rober alongside "Science Bob" Pflugfelder, celebrity guests, and student co-hosts. The initiative was backed by a $7.2 million grant to create the CrunchLabs.org Foundation, a nonprofit "dedicated to revolutionizing science education in a way that promotes critical thinking and inspires lasting curiosity and confidence in STEM," according to a news announcement at the time.

The organization intends to roll out additional courses on YouTube over time, with the ultimate goal of posting more than 1,000 science videos in 34 languages.

Check out the Class CrunchLabs YouTube channel here.

OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI has announced it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a fresh plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.
  • It has been revealed that custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec.
  • For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI has announced it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a fresh plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

It has been revealed that custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the manufacturer indicates timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of newly introduced Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when owners choose to try creating a newly introduced Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

According to recent reports, under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

For organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A company could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

OpenAI states creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

Not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

Sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT people do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

Industry observers note that openAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the company notes, recommending that users retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

It has been revealed that that warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

Sources indicate that despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages users can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

AI-powered vulnerability research is contributing to a major increase in security updates, raising concerns that IT teams could fall behind as patching demands grow, according to cybersecurity firm ThreatDown.

Unauthorized artificial intelligence tools and agents are creating security risks for organizations as AI adoption increases, according to cybersecurity company Sophos.

In its latest threat intelligence report, Ontinue found that attackers are increasingly using trusted workplace tools to trick users into giving them access to enterprise networks.

A vendor coalition built on an Okta-developed blueprint is proposing a shared architecture for discovering, governing, monitoring, and containing enterprise AI agents.

#54883. AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (772 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
  • The research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years.
  • The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

The research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

Recent findings suggest that all respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

In a recent development, on the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents remarked they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

The picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% stated they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to rapidly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

Sources indicate that those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

In a recent development, A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents said such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

According to recent reports, another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they said would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

Arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt newly introduced AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

"Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," stated Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability.".

The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor.
  • Industry observers note that fall has the singular ability to turn even the most Spartan man into a bit of a style savant.
  • It has been revealed that it’s because fall invites more—more layers, more textures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Industry observers note that fall has the singular ability to turn even the most Spartan man into a bit of a style savant. It’s like a wolf awakens the second that temperatures start to drop. Suddenly you see an Instagram post from the junior analyst below you; he must fancy himself a budding A$AP Rocky, because he’s rocking a statement scarf. Your brother-in-law is wearing a turtleneck. Your buddy is in white jeans. Every day, you zone out in dumb stakeholder meetings and fantasize about a upcoming jacket or that pair of buttery-soft leather loafers you saw on a dude at the grocery store.

It has been revealed that it’s because fall invites more—more layers, more textures. It can be freeing. No more worrying if that T-shirt will become a body scan of where and how you sweat; no more worrying if those pants will suffocate you. But ... it can be too much. How should you layer? How can you get funky for the holiday party without looking like an asshole? What brands are even worth buying?

In a recent development, we answer all those questions elsewhere in this magazine, but today we want you to take a breath. Keep it simple. How? By following some good examples.

Sources indicate that A lot of the best-dressed guys right now are trimming down their wardrobes in favor of focusing on the basics. “This fall I’ve tried to trim the fat and make do with a much smaller wardrobe,” states actor, content creator, and friend of the magazine Albert Muzquiz—better known online by his handle @edgyalbert. “I only have a few shirts, a few pants, and a couple jackets—and I feel like I’m dressing better than ever.”.

In a recent development, so instead of lobbing a bunch of meaningless trends, or -cores, at you, we decided to send you to some of the best-dressed men of the moment. You’ve heard enough from us; here’s what they’re feeling this fall.

In a recent development, jake Mueser, founder of the eponymous bespoke suiting brand J. Mueser, has a handful of fall essentials. That cohort includes a cream turtleneck, which “you can throw on with anything,” as well as a classic tweed or herringbone blazer—same idea. They’re easy but plenty damn sexy.

Mueser also extols the virtues of a classic flannel suit—perhaps like the one he makes. “It works with everything from a denim shirt to a tie,” he says. “I like to break it up, wearing the jacket with vintage light-wash Wrangler cowboy cuts.” (A move we wholeheartedly endorse.).

Recent findings suggest that J. Mueser Waverly Herringbone Virgin Wool-Tweed Blazer.

J. Mueser Ivory Chunky Merino Roll-Neck Sweater.

In a recent development, J. Mueser Charcoal Churchill Stripe Flannel Waverly Suit.

There are a few reasons Drew Thomas can’t stop recommending merino sweaters—the thin, almost jersey sort—to his more than 500,000 TikTok followers. “You can get so much wear out of one,” he says. “You can layer it in the fall, wear it on its own on a slightly warmer day, or tie it around your shoulders. It works in the spring too, and even on a summer night when it gets a little cooler.”.

It has been revealed that another seasonally versatile piece Thomas will stand ten toes down for is cream pants. In fact, Thomas likes to wear his all through fall. He keeps a few pairs on constant rotation. “I feel like the cream breaks up those darker fall colors and lets them stand out more,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to his next fall investment, Thomas is taking cues from the British sartorial invasion (“It never really went away, but it definitely feels like it’s having a moment again”) and looking to Barbour. “Something timeless and practical that I can wear for years and that only gets better with age,” he claims. “I love the idea of owning something that develops character over time and could eventually be passed down to someone else. Those are the kinds of pieces I feel are worth investing in.”.

Buck Mason Hollywood Pleated Trouser.

Recent findings suggest that J. Crew Relaxed-Fit Double-Pleated Corduroy Pant.

“A down vest is my favorite fall garment,” Esquire contributor Christopher Fenimore told us. “It’s an easy outerwear piece to layer stuff under. I run hot, and I like having parts of my body exposed to the elements.”.

We second that, but more predictably he highlights the entire category of shirting. Jackets and layers get a lot of shine, but this is the layer that, no matter how much temperatures fluctuate, will be on the skin. It’s a great time to get a few good oxford-cloth button-downs, polos, or beefier tees.

In a recent development, this time of year is also a great time to get clinical. “I assess things I have that might need updates, in terms of fit and silhouette or different fabrications depending on how I’d wear them,” he notes. That can be rebuying your preferred undershirt or socks, or it could be a good time to jump on that thinner, more versatile merino sweater wave.

Rocky Mountain Featherbed Down Vest.

“Fall is the best time to break in a fresh pair of denim,” Muzquiz says. Wear it hard enough now and “it’ll be soft enough and possibly breathable enough for wear during the spring and parts of the summer.” No better time to get something esoteric.

When it comes to fall shoes, Muzquiz is into a classic six-inch lace-up boot. “There are so many bullshit brands out there that are trying to fool you with budget options,” he says. “Just get a pair of Red Wing Heritage if you’re starting out or Viberg if you really wanna flex.”.

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty.
  • The Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI.
  • The research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty. Forty percent of survey respondents cited a lack of specialized infrastructure required by AI as a main challenge to adopting a formal AI strategy, up from 9% in the company's 2024 research.

The Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI. Half of respondents host AI models in private clouds, 86% are pursuing or exploring sovereign AI, 92% tie data-location strategy to their AI prepares, and 88% follow a distributed-data approach.

The research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov. 23, 2025, through Feb. 4, 2026.

Organizations also appear to be shifting from AI planning toward execution. The share actively executing AI to achieve operational efficiency or reduce costs rose from 27% in 2024 to 37% this year. Only 3% reported no measurable ROI to date, while 63% expect returns within the next six months to two years.

According to recent reports, specialized infrastructure led the survey's list of AI adoption challenges at 40%, followed by regulatory and personal-data concerns at 35%. Data availability and quality, storage capacity, interconnection, compute resources, and staffing also ranked as significant constraints.

Those requirements are also shaping workload placement. Integration with existing IT or data infrastructure ranked first at 43%, while regulatory compliance and performance were each cited by 37%. Data proximity, sovereignty, sustainability, cost, and intellectual property protection also factored into hosting decisions.

Private cloud features prominently across the report's AI hosting categories, but enterprises are clearly using a mix of private cloud, public cloud, on-premises infrastructure, and colocation. Private cloud accounted for 50% of custom-built AI model hosting and 47% for open source or fine-tuned large language models (LLMs).

Sovereignty is another part of that placement decision. Thirty-two percent consider sovereign AI — in which data and AI models remain within a single national or regulatory jurisdiction — a requirement, while another 54% are exploring it. The findings point toward hybrid environments in which infrastructure location, governance and data control increasingly overlap.

AI-powered vulnerability research is contributing to a major increase in security updates, raising concerns that IT teams could fall behind as patching demands grow, according to cybersecurity organization ThreatDown.

Unauthorized artificial intelligence tools and agents are creating security risks for organizations as AI adoption increases, according to cybersecurity company Sophos.

In its latest threat intelligence report, Ontinue found that attackers are increasingly using trusted workplace tools to trick users into giving them access to enterprise networks.

A vendor coalition built on an Okta-developed blueprint is proposing a shared architecture for discovering, governing, monitoring, and containing enterprise AI agents.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: OpenAI Intros Dots, AI Agents that Continue Working Between User Conversations

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating users' feedback as they go.
  • It has been revealed that openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities.
  • Industry observers note that the broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating users' feedback as they go.

It has been revealed that openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities. Those enterprise deployments are beginning with focused pilots. The company is working with Microsoft on integration with Agent 365's governance and security controls.

Industry observers note that the broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session. That change could reduce the need to repeatedly explain a project. It also makes supervision a continuing obligation: An instruction that was appropriate yesterday may no longer fit today's circumstances.

Sources indicate that one key distinction appears in OpenAI's privacy and safety FAQ. Disconnecting an application stops new access through that connection, but does not delete information already incorporated into a Dot's context.

In a recent development, customers presently cannot inspect or directly edit individual Dot memories. Deleting a Dot deletes its own context, while files and conversations it created remain separately stored. Plugin permissions are shared across Dots, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.

Industry observers note that for an organization, that creates two related governance questions: what an agent can retrieve now, and what it already knows. Revoking a connection addresses the first without necessarily resolving the second.

OpenAI's safety account distinguishes authorized tasks that continue in the background from unsolicited "proactive research." The latter uses tools restricted to reading permitted sources. Those research tasks cannot directly send messages, change connected application content, or control a browser or desktop. Any subsequent action must pass the usual rules and checks.

It has been revealed that A separate system, Auto-review, checks certain planned actions against instructions and safety requirements. OpenAI says the agent cannot modify the controls enforcing those checks.

"Dots can still make mistakes," the manufacturer cautions.

OpenAI's Dots system-card appendix acknowledges that persistence and multi-agent systems are not upcoming. Its evaluations examine how continuing work affects authorization boundaries.

Recent findings suggest that in one test involving successive related tasks, moderate scope violations increased from 8.6% to 19.7% when the number of intervening tasks doubled from five to 10. Examples included carrying information between unrelated tasks or editing a shared document beyond the intended scope. The company reported no severe breaches or exfiltration in that evaluation.

According to recent reports, these are controlled test results, not measured failure rates in customer deployments. They nevertheless identify a problem that a successful demonstration cannot settle: whether an agent keeps the right boundaries as its workload accumulates.

In a recent development, according to OpenAI's DevDay recap, Dots are available to Pro and Business Premium people in eligible markets. Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare access is an administrator-enabled beta, off by default.

It has been revealed that the operational question is how organizations will keep delegated authority current. A continuing assignment needs a human owner who can revise its scope and decide when to stop it. Otherwise, the convenience of leaving work with an agent can outlast the reason it was authorized.

For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

Industry News: 11 Winter Colognes You Can Get for Under $100

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s never been a better time to get into personal fragrance.
  • In a recent development, so out with the fresh, aquatic, citrusy fragrances that belong on the beach and in with the warm, spicy, smoky scents that make the wintertime feel cozy.
  • If you’ve checked out any of our other affordable-cologne roundups, you won’t be surprised to see Cremo at the top of our list here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s never been a better time to get into personal fragrance. The cologne market is booming with frequent newly introduced rolls out from luxury fashion houses and perfumeries, yes—but it’s also filled with tons of great scents from more accessible and affordable brands. And with the temperatures finally dropping below 50°F in New York and Thanksgiving coming up next week, we’re officially in winter mode. That means getting our puffer coats out of storage and changing up our seasonal fragrance rotation.

In a recent development, so out with the fresh, aquatic, citrusy fragrances that belong on the beach and in with the warm, spicy, smoky scents that make the wintertime feel cozy. We’re talking cardamom and cloves, smoky tobacco and incense, sweet vanilla and smooth amber. Want to capture the scent of sitting by the fireplace and sipping a hot cocoa while wearing a cashmere sweater? These scents will do that—and at a fraction of the cost of a designer fragrance. We rounded up our picks for the winter that all come in at under $100, so you can save the substantial bucks for holiday shopping.

If you’ve checked out any of our other affordable-cologne roundups, you won’t be surprised to see Cremo at the top of our list here. We talk about the brand a lot, but it’s for a good reason: Cremo’s colognes are some of our favorites out there, and they literally cost under $25 each. Spice & Black Vanilla is our favorite spicy scent from the lineup, and the warm blend of cardamom, vanilla, tobacco, and woods is perfect for winter. Wear it for a cold-weather date night, a fancy dinner, or really any occasion.

It has been revealed that want a decent cologne mist you can easily buy on Amazon for just $13? Old Spice has been around for almost 90 years—yes, it may remind you of your dad, but it’s been around for so long because it’s a classic that just works. But shaking things up a bit, the brand released a new collection of cologne mists earlier this year, which includes this Cashmere & Vanilla Wood scent bursting with spices and powdery iris. For $13, you might as well order a few.

One of our favorite boozy colognes (and all-time favorite colognes in general) is Jazz Club from Maison Margiela’s Replica line. It’s one you’ve probably heard of and read about many times in our fragrance roundups, and since the 1 oz bottle is only $89, I just couldn’t leave it off this list. With rum, tobacco, and vanilla bean at the center, Jazz Club is the olfactory equivalent of sipping a cocktail in a smoke-filled bar. In other words, it’s the perfect sexy winter scent.

According to recent reports, gap recently introduced a fresh addition to its revitalized fragrance line (originally from the ’90s): Bliss. The gourmand EDP adds some creamy sweetness to the otherwise mostly fresh and earthy collection, and it came just in time for winter. It delights the senses with notes of butterscotch, cocoa bean, coconut milk, and vanilla bourbon, and it’s practically making my mouth water just thinking about it.

It has been revealed that huron has only five different scents, but it’s a true example of a brand that puts quality over quantity. I love each and every one of the brand’s EDPs, and while the marine Sea Salt + Driftwood and Original Citrus + Eucalyptus are both fresh and perfect for the summer, the Sandalwood + Black Pepper fragrance is definitely our winter choice. It’s warm, woody, and spicy, with some airy florals at the heart and rich amber and more woods at the base.

If you like the scent of Tom Ford’s Oud Wood but can’t get past that $300 price tag, we hear you. That’s why House of Twist made Wood No. 28; it’s not exactly Oud Wood, but it’s close enough. And for just $48, we’ll take it. The fragrance is a nice blend of nutty cardamom, oud wood, vanilla, and creamy sandalwood—a combination pretty much anyone can get behind.

Making the cut at $99 is Phlur’s newest fragrance: Heavy Cream. It’s a rich gourmand that’s balanced out by some bright citrus and airy florals at the top and heart of the fragrance, so it doesn’t get too overwhelmingly heavy. It definitely has the notes you’d expect of a fragrance inspired by heavy cream, like vanilla, amber, and creamy musks.

Fine’ry is another one of our go-to brands when it comes to affordable colognes we actually like. And this winter, our top choice from the lineup is Smoke & Leather, which smells like—you guessed it—smoky tobacco and rich leather with some woody undertones. It definitely brings the heat on a cold day.

Boy Smells is known for pairing traditionally masculine and feminine scent notes for truly unisex fragrances that anyone can enjoy. Hinoki Fantôme is a fan favorite thanks to its blend of spices, woods, and smoke, which are underscored by earthy oakmoss, orris, and patchouli. You really can’t put this fragrance in one category, because it spans so many. It’s a complex fragrance that really works, especially for the winter.

According to recent reports, earthy scents are chameleons that can work in any season, so it really just matters what they’re paired with. In the instance of Stetson’s Free Rein from its new Untamed collection, the pairing of earthy notes of wild verbena, sweetgrass, prairie moss, and patchouli with vetiver smoke and red amber makes it a warm, rich fragrance that adds some heat to your cold-weather outfit.

Recent findings suggest that florals are, generally speaking, made for spring and summer—but sometimes you get a gorgeous blend of florals with woods, musks, or amber, and it becomes perfect for wintertime. That’s exactly what Lafco has done with its Golden Morning scent: It’s got light floral notes of apple blossom, lavender, violet leaf, and rose, which all play nicely with a rich, sweet base of woods, honey, amber, and musks.

  • It has been revealed that according to a new survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders stated their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access.
  • That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.
  • The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that according to a new survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders stated their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time. Perhaps more worrying is that only 19% said their organization could detect in real time when an agent last accessed data outside its intended scope.

That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.

The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.

All the organizations were using or piloting AI, while the employees surveyed used at least one AI tool for work.

The problem becomes more consequential as companies move from AI tools that primarily respond to people toward agents capable of taking actions on their behalf.

Eighty-seven percent of IT and security respondents said their organization had experienced or suspected of an incident during the past year in which an AI tool or agent accessed sensitive information beyond what was required for its task.

It has been revealed that delinea's research also suggests companies are giving agents access that can persist longer than necessary. Only 58% of IT and security leaders noted they have mechanisms that automatically revoke or expire AI access when a session ends, and those controls do not necessarily cover every agent or tool. Forty-two percent said many agent credentials remain active until an audit.

Agents also are not always receiving their own narrowly defined permissions. Half of IT leaders said their organizations use the employee's existing permissions as a boundary for what an agent can access. That can effectively hand an agent years of accumulated access belonging to the person who launched it.

That is particularly significant because an AI agent does not necessarily behave like a traditional service account. A service account typically performs a predefined process, while an agent can choose different tools, actions and sequences at runtime depending on the situation.

Sources indicate that "Service accounts run fixed scripts," said Mike Albrecht, associate director in the Risk Advisory Practice at Cross Country Consulting. "An AI agent decides what actions it's going to take at runtime.".

The enforcement problem is not limited to autonomous agents.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that 76% of employees surveyed had bypassed formal approval at some point to use AI tools with manufacturer data, applications or systems. And 48% remarked they always or extensively use AI tools without going through formal approval.

Meanwhile, 60% noted they had felt pressure to use AI with sensitive or confidential information even when they were not sure doing so was permitted.

Executives were particularly likely to circumvent the process. Eighty-one percent of C-level respondents said they always or regularly bypass AI access approval, compared with 33% of intermediate-level employees.

The result is a widening gap between written AI governance and what companies can see and control. Delinea found that only 41% of IT leaders stated all AI tools and agents accessing tech giant data are actively monitored. When an AI tool or agent went outside its intended scope, 55% said it took at least a day to detect the incident, while 30% said detection took four days or longer.

That suggests the next phase of enterprise AI governance may depend less on writing additional rules and more on whether organizations can enforce existing ones while an agent is working.

"Most organizations cannot confidently answer three questions: What agents are running in our environment? What can they access? What have they actually done?" mentioned Delinea CEO Art Gilliland. "An agent can begin a session with legitimate access and drift into something it was never meant to do.".

The full report is available for download here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic's newly introduced Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation.
  • According to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude.
  • Industry observers note that the organization identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic's newly introduced Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation. Higher-risk tasks can fall back to Sonnet 5.

According to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude. Users receive a notice, and the answer is labeled with the model that provided it. The chat then stays on Sonnet 5 unless the user changes the selection.

Industry observers note that the organization identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks. Source-code vulnerability scanning remains supported. Biology and reasoning-extraction safeguards can block requests outright, rather than route them elsewhere.

Sources indicate that the distinction matters operationally. A block stops the request; a fallback allows an attempt to continue with a different model. Neither outcome should be treated as interchangeable with completion by the model the user originally chose.

Anthropic indicates Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can reduce cost per task by up to 30%, based on its testing. Token prices remain unchanged.

Those claims describe performance under the company's test conditions. An organization evaluating the service also needs to examine what happens when its own assignments encounter safeguards.

Sources indicate that an internal pilot could record how often work is interrupted, whether fallback answers are usable, and when people need help. Such measurements would give buyers a more relevant basis for deployment than assuming every task receives the advertised model's capabilities.

Anthropic has revealed plans to expand its Cyber Verification Program with tiered access for Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Mythos models. Its current program guidance explicitly excludes the two new 5.5 models and says the expansion is forthcoming.

Organizations should distinguish those planned arrangements from access available today.

Industry observers note that the broader enterprise matter is accountability. When an AI service changes models during an assignment, someone still needs to determine whether the resulting work is suitable. A visible handoff helps, but organizations must decide how employees should respond to it.

For more information on Sonnet 5.5, go to the Anthropic site.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.
  • The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies.
  • Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures. The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report: Quantum & AI Trends, based on responses from 3,120 security and IT management professionals across 20 countries, found that 98% are considering how the two technologies affect each other. Thirty percent reported a significant increase in security budgets specifically for AI.

The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies. Fifty-seven percent believe quantum computing will enhance machine learning, while 54% expect it to enable advanced simulations of complex systems. The security findings span data governance, cloud infrastructure, and preparations for quantum-resistant encryption.

Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively. The report connects that exposure to the large datasets required for AI training and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Organizations are also looking to cloud providers for protection: 67% reported investing in their cloud provider's AI-specific security tools, compared with 63% using an established security provider. Respondents could identify multiple sources of protection, including startups, large language model providers, and internally developed controls.

Industry observers note that encryption coverage remains incomplete. Only 7% of organizations reported encrypting more than 80% of their sensitive cloud data, while 29% reported encrypting more than 60%. The report's chart puts the average share encrypted at 47% in 2026, down from 51% in 2025.

The findings extend concerns raised in coverage of Thales' 2025 cloud security research, when AI security already ranked second to cloud security in spending priorities and 52% of respondents reported that AI security spending was displacing existing security budgets. The latest report again places AI security second, while its historical comparison shows average sensitive cloud data encryption coverage falling from 51% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

According to recent reports, AI security was the second-highest prioritized security spending category overall, behind cloud security. But protecting data ranked much lower among the measures organizations use to judge AI projects: Reducing or managing risks of data loss or noncompliance placed sixth among seven success criteria, at 35%.

Improving customer experience led those measures at 68%, followed by reducing employee toil through greater task automation at 63%. Meanwhile, poor data quality or initial data governance was the leading inhibitor to AI adoption, cited by 65%; security risks from exposed data followed at 61%. Another 51% cited AI initiatives moving too swiftly to be properly secured.

Latest Update: Flashpoint Receives Patent for Ransomware Risk Model, Tying Vulnerabilites to Likelihood of Attack

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cybersecurity firm Flashpoint revealed it has received U.S.
  • The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.
  • Industry observers note that of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cybersecurity firm Flashpoint revealed it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.

Industry observers note that of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code. Flashpoint also reported a 45 percent increase in Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) attacks during the period.

It has been revealed that the patent was granted August 11 2026, although the underlying Ransomware Risk model isn't fresh. It has been available through Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence since 2022.

The model addresses a basic vulnerability-management problem: severity and real-world ransomware risk aren't necessarily the same thing, because severity scores do not necessarily indicate which flaws attackers are most likely to target.

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, measures how severe a vulnerability could be. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, estimates the probability of exploitation more broadly.

Flashpoint's Ransomware Risk model adds another dimension by comparing newly disclosed vulnerabilities with the characteristics of flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks.

Industry observers note that that could change where a vulnerability lands in an organization's patching queue. A lower-severity flaw might normally sit behind numerous critical vulnerabilities. But if its characteristics closely resemble vulnerabilities repeatedly targeted by ransomware operators, security teams may have reason to move it higher.

Sources indicate that "A severity score alone can't tell you which vulnerabilities pose the greatest real-world risk of exploitation by ransomware actors," Flashpoint CEO Josh Lefkowitz remarked. "Our patented Ransomware Risk model applies years of threat intelligence to that problem, giving customers an earlier signal and helping them prioritize based on how attackers actually operate.".

Industry observers note that the firm's midyear research also illustrates the scale of the prioritization problem. Its vulnerability intelligence covers traditional IT systems as well as cloud, IoT, operational technology, open source software. and third-party libraries.

The manufacturer indicates it also tracks more than 105,000 vulnerabilities that aren't represented in CVE or the National Vulnerability Database, expanding the pool of flaws that security teams may need to evaluate.

The cybersecurity company's patented methodology profiles vulnerabilities using more than 60 technical characteristics, including whether a flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication, whether it affects operational technology systems, and how exploitation could affect data availability.

Those characteristics form a multi-factor fingerprint. The model maps each vulnerability against clusters containing flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks and assigns a Low, Medium, High, or Critical Ransomware Risk rating.

Flashpoint claims the rating can be generated when a vulnerability is disclosed, rather than requiring security teams to wait for public evidence of active exploitation. Ratings are then updated as newly introduced ransomware activity and threat intelligence emerge.

According to recent reports, within Flashpoint Ignite, Ransomware Risk appears alongside CVSS, EPSS, Social Risk, and exploit maturity. The idea isn't to replace existing scoring systems, but to give administrators additional information when deciding what to remediate first.

Industry observers note that nor does a High or Critical Ransomware Risk rating mean a vulnerability will necessarily be exploited. The model measures how closely its characteristics resemble vulnerabilities historically associated with ransomware attacks.

For security teams facing thousands of potential vulnerabilities, that distinction matters. The flaw carrying the highest severity score isn't necessarily the one that most closely resembles what ransomware operators have historically chosen to attack.

"Despite being the most popular indicator for priority, we know that severity alone doesn't tell you whether a vulnerability will be exploited or used in ransomware," said Ben Haynes, Data Science & Analytics Lead at Flashpoint and co-inventor of the patented methodology.

"A vulnerability can score low on a traditional severity scale and still share the characteristics we repeatedly see in ransomware attacks.".
